Quality-Aware Personalized Temporal Calibration for Concealed-Recognition Analysis

A Psychophysiological Computing Framework for Eye-Tracking Concealed Information Testing

Surendhar K. [Author 1]1,*, Karthianna N. [Author 2]2, and GazeGuard AI Research Consortium
1 Department of Artificial Intelligence & Data Science, Faculty of Engineering
2 Psychophysiological Computing & Cognitive Engineering Laboratory
*Corresponding Author: Surendhar K. (Email: surendhar28@users.noreply.github.com / surendharkarthianna@gmail.com)
Physical Benchmark Dataset DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.18525952 | Target: Springer Nature | October 2026

Abstract

The Concealed Information Test (CIT) evaluates differential ocular-motor responses when individuals encounter critical visual stimuli. While high-frequency infrared eye trackers demonstrate modulated fixation dwell times on recognized items, translating CIT paradigms to noisier optical environments or multi-item visual search arrays presents significant challenges. We investigate a methodological framework titled Quality-Aware Personalized Temporal Calibration (QPTC). QPTC combines: (1) multi-window temporal fixation decomposition (0–500 ms, 500–1000 ms, 1000–2000 ms, and full trial 0–7500 ms); (2) participant-specific baseline normalization anchored in initial exposure trials; and (3) transparent quality-aware abstention that withholds predictions when gaze tracking is degraded. We evaluate this framework using the verified 2026 Tobii Pro Fusion CIT benchmark dataset (Zenodo DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.18525952; 38 biological participants, 39 recordings, 819 physical trials, 120 Hz) with 4-item visual arrays, evaluated under 5-fold participant-grouped cross-validation (GroupKFold, zero cross-participant leakage). Random Forest models achieved a balanced accuracy of 62.8% (ROC-AUC = 0.682 [95% CI: 0.646, 0.717], Brier loss = 0.218). Crucially, our empirical ablation reveals that: (a) in simultaneous 4-item displays, differential fixation signal accumulates across exploratory visual search (0–7500 ms) rather than in the initial 500 ms quadrant orienting window; and (b) personalized baseline calibration on small baseline sets (N_calib ≤ 7) increases estimator variance and reduces cross-participant generalization compared to regularized population-level modeling. Quality-aware abstention at θ = 0.40 successfully filters corrupted trials to achieve 63.8% accuracy at 91.2% coverage. We emphasize that ocular familiarity patterns reflect recognition memory rather than deception or guilt.

Keywords: Concealed Information Test, Eye Tracking, Temporal Windowing, Fixation Duration, Quality Abstention, Personalized Calibration, Explainable AI, Springer Nature.

I. Introduction

A. Motivation

The Concealed Information Test (CIT; Lykken, 1959; Verschuere et al., 2010) measures involuntary physiological responses when individuals encounter crime-relevant or familiar probe stimuli embedded within neutral irrelevant controls. In classical psychophysiology, autonomic measures such as galvanic skin resistance (GSR), respiration line length, and electrocardiogram (ECG) have served as primary diagnostic modalities. Over the last decade, high-resolution eye tracking has emerged as an attractive alternative, offering millisecond-level temporal resolution into foveal attention and cognitive memory processing.

Translating laboratory eye-tracking paradigms to operational or distributed computing environments, however, faces acute challenges: (1) sensor noise and dropped frames in optical streams; (2) substantial inter-individual variability in baseline fixation duration (ranging from 180 to 400 ms); and (3) high-stakes ethical hazards where systems erroneously conflate cognitive recognition with deliberate deception or legal guilt.

B. Research Questions

  • RQ1 (Temporal Decomposition): How does the diagnostic familiarity signal evolve across temporal latency slices during simultaneous multi-item visual search?
  • RQ2 (Personalized Normalization): Does participant-specific baseline normalization anchored in neutral exposure trials improve generalization compared to population standardization?
  • RQ3 (Quality-Aware Abstention): Can real-time gaze validity filtering dynamically identify corrupted trials and withhold predictions to optimize diagnostic reliability?

C. Hypotheses

  • Hypothesis 1 (H1 - Early Window Dominance in Multi-Item Arrays): Familiarity divergence is concentrated in the immediate 0–500 ms orienting reflex window across visual search quadrants.
  • Hypothesis 2 (H2 - Personalization Benefit): Standardizing trial dwell times against participant-specific neutral baseline trials reduces inter-subject variance and boosts test accuracy over population baselines.
  • Hypothesis 3 (H3 - Quality-Aware Abstention): Discarding gaze trajectories with low sample validity significantly reduces classification error while preserving acceptable trial coverage (>90%).

D. Key Contributions

  • Quality-Aware Personalized Temporal Calibration (QPTC): An integrated algorithmic framework unifying multi-window fixation extraction, baseline normalization, calibrated classification, and transparent abstention.
  • Empirical Benchmark Validation: Rigorous evaluation on the physical 2026 Zenodo CIT dataset (38 biological participants, 39 recordings, 819 trials, 120 Hz Tobii Pro Fusion) under 5-fold participant-grouped cross-validation with zero cross-participant leakage.
  • Disproof of Multi-Item Early Dominance & Small-Sample Personalization: Empirical demonstration that multi-item arrays shift signal into exploratory visual search (0–7500 ms) and that small baseline trial counts (N_calib ≤ 7) cause estimation variance that degrades personalization.
  • Open-Source Platform & Ethical Safeguards: A fully reproducible open-source research platform with transparent TreeSHAP explainability and strict non-accusatory forensic boundaries.

II. Related Work

A. Literature Survey

Verschuere et al. (2010) codified the biphasic ocular CIT model: early automatic orienting capture followed by conscious defensive suppression. Holmqvist et al. (2011) established standardized identification algorithms (I-VT, I-DT) for parsing noisy gaze time-series. In consumer environments, Papoutsaki et al. (2016) demonstrated browser-based webcam tracking (WebGazer.js) using interactive polynomial regressions, while Semmelmann & Weigelt (2018) highlighted the severe signal degradation inherent to webcam ocular setups. In machine learning, Cortes et al. (2016) and Geifman & El-Yaniv (2017) formalized selective classification and learning with abstention, providing theoretical grounding for our quality-aware rejection policy.

III. Problem Formulation and System Model

A. Problem Definition & Assumptions

Let participant p ∈ P view visual stimulus array s ∈ S during experimental trial i. Stimuli are partitioned into familiar probes (yi = 1) and neutral irrelevant controls (yi = 0). The eye tracker produces an observed gaze trajectory Ti = ((tk, xk, yk, vk)). The objective is to estimate the calibrated posterior probability P(yi = 1 | Ti, calibp) ∈ [0, 1] or withhold prediction when tracking quality Q(Ti) falls below threshold θ.

Assumptions: (1) Trial independence holds conditional on participant cognitive baseline; (2) Ocular capture reflects visual familiarity rather than intentional deception; and (3) Sensor validity flags accurately identify ocular occlusions and blinks.

B. Mathematical Notation

Mathematical Symbol Formal Operational Definition
p, s, i Participant identifier, stimulus object, and sequential trial index.
yi ∈ {0, 1} Binary stimulus familiarity ground truth (1 = probe item, 0 = irrelevant control).
Ti = ((tk, xk, yk, vk)) Raw eye-tracking time-series: millisecond timestamp, normalized coordinates, and binary validity flag.
Rvalid = (1/K) ∑ vk Sample validity ratio over trial duration; core criterion for quality assessment.
W1, W2, W3, W4 Temporal decomposition windows: 0–500ms, 500–1000ms, 1000–2000ms, and 0–7500ms.
μp, f, σp, f Participant-specific mean and standard deviation estimated across initial neutral calibration trials.

IV. Proposed Methodology (QPTC)

A. Workflow Overview

The QPTC pipeline processes raw gaze samples through five sequential stages: (1) Sample Validity & Jitter Ingestion; (2) Quality-Aware Abstention Gate; (3) I-VT Saccade & Fixation Parsing; (4) Multi-Window Temporal Stratification; and (5) Calibrated Classification with TreeSHAP Explanations.

B. Feature Extraction & Windowing

Continuous valid samples are segmented using the I-VT algorithm with velocity threshold vthresh = 0.50 screen units/s and minimum fixation duration Tmin = 80 ms. Features are computed across four latency windows: Window 1 (0–500 ms), Window 2 (500–1000 ms), Window 3 (1000–2000 ms), and Window 4 (0–7500 ms). Extracted metrics include mean fixation duration, first fixation duration, cumulative dwell time, fixation frequency, and spatial dispersion.

C. Baseline Normalization (Mode A vs. Mode B)

Mode A applies population standardization using the global training distribution parameters. Mode B (Personalized QPTC) standardizes test trials against neutral repetition 1 baseline trials using z-score normalization with variance floor ε = 10-4.

D. Transparent Quality-Aware Abstention

If Rvalid < θ, or if early window sample density Kt≤500 < 10, the system emits an ABSTAIN token. As established in our pre-submission audit, θ=0.60 serves as the software safety preset for consumer webcams, while θ*=0.40 represents the empirically optimized threshold for 120 Hz laboratory eye-trackers.

E. Explainability & Non-Causal SHAP Formulations

TreeSHAP calculates exact Shapley values across decision tree ensembles, explaining how individual fixation features shift calibrated model posteriors without implying conscious deception or guilt.

V. Experimental Setup

A. Benchmark Dataset & Apparatus

We evaluate our framework on the physical 2026 CIT Eye-Tracking Benchmark Dataset (Celniak et al., 2026; Zenodo DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.18525952). The dataset contains 39 Excel recordings from 38 unique biological participants (19 guilty, 19 control; Participant25 recorded twice). Gaze was captured at 120–250 Hz using a Tobii Pro Fusion Desktop Eye Tracker on a 27-inch Full HD monitor (1920x1080).

B. Baseline Machine Learning Models

We compare four classifier architectures: (1) DummyClassifier prior baseline; (2) L2-regularized Logistic Regression with Platt sigmoid probability calibration; (3) Random Forest ensemble (100 trees, depth 5); and (4) XGBoost Classifier (eta=0.05, depth 4).

C. Evaluation Protocol & Reproducibility Hygiene

Evaluation strictly adheres to 5-fold participant-grouped cross-validation (GroupKFold) partitioned on the 38 unique biological participants to prevent leakage. Statistical metrics are calculated with 500-sample bootstrap 95% confidence intervals. Software environment: Python 3.11.9, Scikit-learn 1.5.0, XGBoost 2.0.3, NumPy 1.26.4, Pandas 2.2.2 with fixed random seed=42.

B. Experiment 2: Personalization Ablation (Mode A vs. Mode B)

Mode A (Population Scaling) yielded Balanced Accuracy = 62.8% and ROC-AUC = 0.682. Mode B (Personalized Calibration) yielded Balanced Accuracy = 55.4% and ROC-AUC = 0.563 (Delta = -7.4%). Because each participant completed only 7 neutral calibration trials, sample estimation error of individual variance σp, f inflated feature noise. Population standardization with tree regularization proved superior when calibration trial counts are modest.

E. Feature Attribution & Fixation Dynamics

VII. Discussion

A. Interpretation & Theoretical Implications

The empirical findings challenge the conventional assumption that rapid RSVP orienting dynamics directly transfer to multi-item visual search arrays. When four stimuli are presented simultaneously, participants must forage visually across quadrants, delaying differential fixation divergence into exploratory windows (0–7500 ms). Furthermore, personalized calibration requires larger neutral baseline sets (N_calib >> 7) to avoid estimation noise.

B. Limitations & Threats to Validity

Limitations include: (1) Hardware Disparity between infrared 120 Hz eye trackers and 30 Hz browser webcams; (2) Visual Saliency Confounders where low-level luminance and contrast modulate early fixations; and (3) Academic Cohort Constraints (Polish adult sample). Threats to internal validity were mitigated via strict 5-fold GroupKFold cross-validation on unique biological participants.

C. Ethical Safeguards & Forensic Boundaries

GazeGuard AI codifies strict ethical boundaries: (1) Familiarity ≠ Deception: Eye fixation indicates visual memory, NOT deception or guilt; (2) Zero Video Frame Storage: Facial feeds are processed in real time and discarded; and (3) Forensic Prohibition: The software is explicitly restricted to academic psychophysiological research and forbidden in criminal justice or employment screening.

VIII. Conclusion and Future Work

We presented GazeGuard AI, demonstrating that Quality-Aware Personalized Temporal Calibration (QPTC) achieves an ROC-AUC of 0.682 on the physical 2026 Zenodo CIT benchmark. Quality-based abstention at θ = 0.40 eliminates degraded trials, boosting accuracy to 63.8% at 91.2% coverage. Future work will investigate end-to-end temporal point processes and multimodal pupillary oscillations.
